deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate research problems from Hilbert's problem notebook. None contains a worked derivation.

(1) Conclusion of the problem from the previous page. Determine the number of primes p ≤ X for which 2 is a primitive root mod p, and above all prove there are infinitely many such primes. Hilbert's hint: apply Chebyshev's methods (a book reference 'S. 306', most likely Chebyshev's prime-counting estimates as presented in some textbook). In modern terms: estimate #{p ≤ X : ord_p(2) = p−1} and prove it is infinite. This is the base-2 case of what is now Artin's primitive root conjecture. Chebyshev-type elementary methods are not known to suffice; the conditional answer (on GRH) is ~ A·π(X) with Artin's constant A ≈ 0.3739 (Hooley 1967).

(2) Programme to axiomatize mechanics, then optics, electricity theory etc., 'exactly as was done with the axioms of geometry'. The tasks are:
- identify precisely the experiments underlying each axiom and describe the whole range of phenomena;
- prove why a different axiom system describes the phenomena worse;
- carry out this last comparison first for geometry.
This is a programmatic statement, not a derivation. It is a direct precursor of the 6th Paris problem (1900).

(3) Let y be an algebraic function of x, F(x,y)=0, with branches y_1(x),...,y_n(x). Consider the locus C = {x ∈ ℂ : |y_i(x)| = |y_j(x)| for some i≠j}. With x = u+iv this is a real one-dimensional set in the (u,v)-plane. Hilbert claims:
- C is an algebraic curve;
- branch points lie at double points of C, though (next page) not every double point is a branch point.
The continuation on the next page orders the roots by modulus and labels each arc of C (cut at its double points) with i when the i-th and (i+1)-th roots have equal modulus. He claims this labelled scheme replaces the Riemann surface, i.e. the sheet/monodromy scheme can be recovered from it (cf. Runge, Fritz Cohn).

My local analysis (not on the page): near a simple branch point x0 put x−x0 = s². Then y_{1,2} = a ± b s + c s² + ..., and
|y_1|² − |y_2|² = 4 Re( conj(b s)(a + c s² + ...) ),
which is an odd function of s. Its zero set is a smooth curve through s=0 that is symmetric under s → −s, so its image in the x-plane is a single arc ending at x0. The worked example y = 1 ± √x gives C = (−∞, 0], a ray ending at the branch point 0.
errors: 'Algebraic curve' is loose. The true locus is defined by a modulus condition in which conj(y_i) must be paired with y_i. It is in general only real semi-algebraic. Its Zariski closure contains spurious pieces: for y = 1 ± √x the locus is the ray x ≤ 0, but its closure is the whole real axis.

The claim that branch points lie at double points is not correct generically. For a simple branch point with nonzero branch value, the locus |y_1| = |y_2| near x0 is a single arc emanating from x0, so x0 is an endpoint, not a crossing. In the Zariski closure the local equation is (Im(w² (x−x0)))² = 0, a doubled line, so the 'double point' description holds only in a degenerate sense.

Degenerate cases are not excluded. If the branches satisfy y_j = −y_i identically (e.g. y² = p(x)), then |y_i| = |y_j| everywhere and the locus is the whole plane. Some genericity assumption is needed.

The hint that Chebyshev's elementary methods would prove infinitude of primes with primitive root 2 is over-optimistic. The problem remains open unconditionally; it is known only on GRH (Hooley 1967), and Heath-Brown (1986) proved that at most two primes fail to be primitive roots for infinitely many p.

deep.surprise_reason: The physics-axiomatization entry is a known precursor of the 6th problem, and Corry discusses Hilbert's notebooks on this. Posing the primitive-root-2 counting problem decades before Artin is mildly notable, but Gauss already raised related questions. The equal-modulus scheme for Riemann surfaces is an unusual unpublished idea, but it is sketchy and partly incorrect as stated.
